newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Ruling party predicts Cameroon poll victory.
newsitem.headline: Ruling party predicts Cameroon poll victory.

text.p: President Paul Biya's ruling party said on Sunday it would win an outright majority in Cameroon's new parliament.
Opposition parties scaled back projections of the number of seats they expected to win, denouncing fraud and problems their supporters had obtaining voter cards.

Election officials said polling in the Northern Province of the central African state took place on Sunday only after the late arrival of ballot papers. Biya, whose party expected to win 20 of the 29 seats there, had to sign a special decree authorising the belated vote.

Azu'u Fonkam, coordinator of Biya's Cameroon People's Democratic Rally (RDPC) election commission, told Reuters at their headquarters in the capital Yaounde they expected to win up to 102 of the new assembly's 180 seats.
"We will not have less than 92 at worst," he said.
The mood at the Yaounde offices of the opposition Social Democratic Front (SDF), whose leader John Fru Ndi narrowly lost to Biya in a 1992 presidential election, was more sombre.
"I am very pessimistic that we will only get 56 seats," Alhaji Sani, its election coordinator, told Reuters.
"The organisation was catastrophic," he said. "Because of rigging we are very pessimistic. So many people did not get cards."

The mood was the same at the Yaounde offices of the National Union for Democracy and Progress (UNDP), which won 68 seats in 1992. "With the fraud we have revised our projection from 35 to 30 seats," said campaign director Pierre Flambeau Ngayap.

The Front, which boycotted Cameroon's 1992 parliamentary election, has its power base in the volatile English-speaking North-West Province but draws support from Cameroon's main ethnic Bamileke group and the urban poor.
North-West Province is a flashpoint in largely French-speaking Cameroon.
Fru Ndi had predicted the Front would win 100 seats.

Fonkam dismissed talk of fraud, saying there was bound to be some cheating during elections. He said 14,000 of the 39,000 voters in the Front stronghold of Bamenda had registered more than once. One man had registered 11 times, he added.
A total of 45 parties fielded 1,800 candidates for the poll, the second since Cameroon's 1990 multi-party transition.
The interior ministry said it would not issue provisional results. It has 20 days to announce final results.
Biya, who took over from independence president Ahmadou Ahidjo in 1982, faces a presidential election in October.
